title: Here is why most AI games are AI slop
author: Old-Wolverine-4134
selftext:
The problem is not that AI is bad or that the game looks bad. The problem is and always will be the lack of ideas and originality. The more accessible and easy to use a tool becomes, the more people think that things are easy. AI generates video? Oh, so now I can make my own movie. AI can code now? So I can make my own software. AI makes games? So now it's super easy to make my own game. Right?

A big no. Especially in the game industry, the most important thing has been and always will be the idea. You can have the most beautiful game in the world, but if it lacks an idea and originality, it will never succeed. And vice versa, a game can look terrible, but be super original and grab the interest of millions of people.

Here we see many people who are trying to make games, but they all want to go from A to Z, skipping all the other steps in the development of a game.

Don't get me wrong, I'm really happy to see a cool project here, but as you can see, this is rare. Most posts are just attempts with prompts and no idea, story, or any substance whatsoever. Either way, I really hope we start seeing some gems amongst all of these in near future.

honestly, as someone who has as a hobby, "done game development" for close to 20 years, the biggest thing AI has done for me is force me to realize how little time I spent learning actual game design.

I can make some absolutely stellar tools, I can implement graphics code and compute shaders 
like a boss.

Now that I spend far less time on those parts, I'm finding it really hard to actually put together experiences that I find fun, and that other people enjoy, like my kids or game jam folks.

I know fun when I see it, and I have an idea of what the end product needs to look and feel like, but I dont know how to get from concept to end product in terms of game design.  so now thats where I have to spend my time.

comments.author: robhanz
comments.body:
I saw a quote by John Carmack once that said that it's not the big idea that makes or breaks your game - it's all of the tiny little ones you make during development.

I think it's the same with AI.

If you tell AI "make me a box" it has to fill in all of the details - size, material, what it's holding, how to open it, etc.

The more information you give it, the better the box will be.  Not because the AI would make "bad" decisions, but because it doesn't know what you actually want.

And so I think that's what happens.  When you tell AI "make me a game lol" it makes all of those little decisions.  And, at least at this point, AI doesn't know feel.  It doesn't know how to make those little decisions. And I think that if there's an art in game development it's in the loop of "try this, see if it works, make it better, and test it again".  That's why we do grey box and mechanic and level iteration.

Used properly, AI can make a good developer better by letting them do that refinement loop faster and more efficiently and with less cost.  But the idea that it will *remove* that is, to me, silly.  At least at this point in time, who knows about five years from now?  I don't want a one-shot game today.  I want to one-shot something to the point where I can start evaluating and tweaking it and making it better.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
This aligns nicely with my experience. I get frustrated when I see one-shot games that look really good. I ask myself why has it taken me so long to get where I am with my own game.

Then I spend a day like today where I am putting in place the tools to balance the gameplay and ensuring there is a consistent data structure. I also tweaked some small UI items, corrected some visual bugs and added some more depth from an emergent idea. 

It’s through this slower and more considered approach that I believe you create good games. Having the bravery to say no to the AI suggestions, to wrestle back the approval process and to take the time to read all of the requirements. Then you are making a game again, not just watching a computer build its own game.

comments.author: cxfoulke
comments.body:
"always will be the idea" 

Honestly cant disagree more... Ideas are valueless... as someone whos played multiple dozen alphas and game jam games. Visual execution and "feel" matter more than anything else. How you present the game is what matters. 

There are 800 vampire survivor games after the game did well and i can tell you for certain if another one comes out and really nails the game feel it will still pop on steam. 

I've seen so many "cool" ideas of  what if game questions or fun genre twists. But if the visuals/game feel don't match it doesnt matter 99% of the time. 

The real reason is almost always Visual Dissonance. Elements of the game that slightly dont match together that animate in a buggy manner. Its the uncanny valley of game dev that just gives people the ick.  

Like ive seen a bunch of games posted here where they have these super high resolution sprites sitting on ground textures that dont blend correctly and a ui style that is minimalist. The clash puts you off and the "idea" would be fighting the negative emotions. 

If you game jams  feel+visuals+execution almost always win vs cool idea.

Then you got games like doki doki literature club which looks like another dumb romance novel and it went crazy viral, even though it was nothing ground breaking. Messed up horror romance visual novels already existed and Pony Island (I’m sure before Pony Island too) already did the “your computer is messing with you” thing.

comments.author: dazawmbie
comments.body:
Without spoiling too much, I'm working on a VN set around pseudo-Japanese BBSes in the 90s, and I've found generative AI really helpful in realizing the project.

Years ago I wanted to make PC-98-style CG manually, but a single image could take me hours and the results honestly weren't that impressive. With customized generative AI, a conversion/tooling pipeline, and manual editing, I can create much more of that content, much faster, while getting closer to the look I originally had in mind.

The same applies to music and other assets, although I haven't gotten the results there to the same level as the art yet. On the ideas side, I find it useful to brainstorm with AI, take bits and pieces from different directions, and then stitch together and edit them into a more coherent concept.

For me it's less about having AI come up with the game and more about making it feasible to actually realize an idea that would otherwise be very difficult for me to produce on my own.

comments.author: Schwolop
comments.body:
Well you might enjoy my games then, as they’re definitely unique. I’m a tabletop game designer who’s been rejected by publishers so often I had to start my own publishing company to get my games out there. That could be because they’re terrible, but the number of smiles I see would suggest otherwise.

I’m now building digital friendslop versions of my games with AI and having a blast making them. My first is called Crack & Stack and is a cerebral dexterity memory hybrid where you must stack dice in towers while solving and remembering a simple maths, shapes, or wordplay puzzle. All whilst a commentator yells frantically at you that it’s a race and you’d better bloody well hurry up! And now that it’s digital, in addition to the classic tabletop gameplay, I can have all manner of physics engine driven craziness; low-gravity, bouncy dice modes, bonus rounds where you try to catapult down another player’s tower. Oh and there’s a fully realised LED lighting system for the gaming table because fuck it, I had spare tokens, and it made it while I was asleep.

For creatives like me who can do most of what they need to get their ideas out there, but lose motivation when a roadblock gets in the way of the dopamine stream of progress, AI development is addictive and exciting. I can throw shit at the wall and see what sticks. And because I have taste, I can be confident what I keep will be really fun gameplay.

I hope there are more people like me, and we’re about to see a goldmine of awesome new genres of games. (Although we’ll have to wade through a sea of slop to get there…)

comments.author: UnderStrangeStars

"I made a game in 5 minutes" - yeah, everyone can tell.

Making a good game is a labor of love. Even experienced game developers are tweaking, tuning, and iterating. They scrap ideas. The act of building it is slow, but the ideas / movement of letting it ferment on your brain is where the subsequent content comes from. That's why people AI "soulless" -- what is the soul? the "je ne sais quoi"? It's what happens when you spend hours and hours and hours pouring over the minutia.

So I'm not anti-AI but you'll need to make up the time cognitively processing the game elsewhere. It just feels natural to do it while programming / drawing vs playing and prompting.

That's my two cents, and I don't believe in using AI for that reason. I still want to provide advice and support AI game devs... but I find many "devs" are prompting for an hour, slapping it up -- then expecting everyone else to tell them what to do next.

I see it more or less the same way.

Part of being a creator comes down to understanding the body of work well enough to be a good judge of quality.

The biggest problem AI adds to that is just that you can now finish complete works without necessarily knowing if they’re any good or not.

That’s what slop is: a creative work devoid of value.

So the market gets flooded with a bunch of technically complete works put out by the same kind of people who foisted shovelware before.

On the upside, this means shovelware is even more devalued than ever. The technology devastates the low effort market by making it more accessible than ever.

On the downside, it means consumers have even a bigger mountain of slop to sift through in order to find something worthwhile.

However I honestly have no problem with the idea of utilizing the technology in the first place. Thinking AI is responsible for slop existing is just as misguided as thinking making a game in Unity means its slop.

Just because games have become easier to make doesn’t mean people who know what they’re doing can’t use those means to make good games.
